newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila economic signs good, but concerns linger.
newsitem.headline: Manila economic signs good, but concerns linger.

text.p: The Philippine economy's vital signs are good, but this week's de facto devaluation of the Thai baht has led to concerns about the sustainability of exports and Manila's ability to keep inflation down, analysts said on Friday.

"A major review (of export policy) will have to be made because the recent Thai baht devaluation has put the Philippine peso at a price disadvantage," Mike Oyson, a senior analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Securities (Phils) Inc, told Reuters.
The sharp fall of the baht means that Thai exports are cheaper relative to their Philippine counterparts because of the foreign exchange differentials.

There used to be an effective one-for-one exchange rate between the two currencies, but on Friday morning the baht was at 28.20/28.70 per U.S. dollar while the peso was hovering between 26.397 and 26.40.
"The impact will not be immediate, because orders have been made. But why should importers buy from the Philippines if they can get the goods cheaper from Thailand?" Oyson said.
He added the central bank, which has defended the peso from speculative attack, should allow the peso to depreciate to the same level as the baht.

So far this year the Philippines' export performance has been above expectations. On Friday, the National Statistics Office said merchandise exports grew 22.7 percent in the first five months of the year to $9.558 billion.
In May alone, exports rose 22.2 percent to $1.612 billion.
Analysts said this growth strengthened the view that the Philippines was not going the way of Thailand. But with Thailand now at a comparative advantage, Manila's export growth rate could slow.
Earlier this week, two exporters' groups reiterated a long-standing demand for a devaluation of the peso, but the central bank again rejected the demand.
Joy Quintos, head of research at Capitol Securities One, said the spillover from the baht's troubles could fuel inflation in the Philippines.

On Wednesday, within minutes of the Thai government announcing a managed float of the baht the Philippine central bank moved to defend the peso by raising its benchmark overnight interest rate to 24 percent from 15 percent.

"If we see continued speculation in the foreign exchange market, we might see some effect on inflation. The cost of production might go up and companies might pass this on to consumers," Quintos said.
Oyson said price pressures could also creep in later this year when campaigning for the May 1998 presidential elections begins.

Inflation rose to 4.8 percent in June from 4.2 percent the previous month. The figure was slightly higher than the market's expectation of 4.23 percent and way off the Central Bank's projection of 3.9 percent.
But analysts said the increase was not worrisome because it was still within the full-year target of 5.2-5.7 percent.
